_comment: 🧩️ This subset's own contribution. `s.layout.layout` is a semio-NATIVE artifact carried in `.dsl.semio`/`.pack.semio`, so no third party can serve as its reference — see the noOracleDecision below.

noOracleDecisions.rationale: No third-party crate reads or writes semio's `.dsl.semio`/`.pack.semio` envelope, and none is authoritative over `LayoutMutation`. What distinguishes this subset from every sibling is that a layout document is FOUR pools at two nesting depths joined by reference: document-root scalars (`name`, `printTarget`, `dataFieldsJson`), the id-keyed root collections `pages`, `stories` and `links`, and — nested one level down, inside a page — that page's own `layers` and `frames`. A frame is therefore addressed by (page, frame) rather than by id alone, a text frame names its `stories` member by id and an image frame names its `links` member by id, so `delete-story` and `delete-link` reach ACROSS pools into frames that point at them, while `reorder-pages` moves a whole nested subtree. Confidence comes from the committed per-kind specification vectors under `../🧬️schema/🧬️mutations/<kind>/🧪️tests/<fixture>/` — a `(before, mutation, after, diff, outcome)` quintet per kind, already unit-tested inside the production crate — plus the inverse law as a metamorphic property: applying a kind and then its own computed inverse must restore the exact pre-mutation document, including a deleted page's ORIGINAL index and its whole frame subtree, which a deletion undone by re-appending would not. The `mutate-layout-1` case re-exercises those SAME committed bytes end-to-end through `apply_layout_mutation`/`inverse_layout_mutation`.
